name: Adam Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and nothing is used with your name on it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a share-farmer at Kendrick's, which means I bring the cows and the work, Mrs Kendrick brings the land and buildings, and we split the profit. It's a hundred and eighty dairy cows with two milking robots, plus grass and maize for silage. The robots milk the cows whenever the cows choose to walk in, so my day is less about milking and more about watching screens and fixing things. I'm up at five, check the overnight alerts on my phone, then it's feet, fertility, feeding and fences.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does a typical alert look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Cow 212 hasn't been milked in fourteen hours, or her milk conductivity is up, which usually means mastitis starting, that's an infection in the udder. I ask the AI assistant to pull her history and suggest what to check, and it's right more often than I'd have guessed. I use it every day, for feed rations, for the grass plan, even for writing up the monthly report for Mrs Kendrick. My wife Sofia says I talk to it more than I talk to her, which is unfair, but only a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I've already had most of the good bits. The robots and the assistant are the big change on my farm, and they're here now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people who called it hype weren't wrong, but the useful bits are really useful. I'd still tell anyone at the discussion group that a milking robot changed my life. I just wouldn't promise them a revolution.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my life stays good. I'll keep share-farming until sixty-five, the robots keep my back in one piece, and I keep my hands on the cows. Nothing to lose sleep over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do, keep using the AI daily, and maybe try the newer grass-measuring drone if it comes down in price. I'd pay off the last of the loan on the cows, about eight thousand left. Then save harder for retirement, because share-farmers don't get pensions from anybody.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Happy enough. Maybe a bit bored at the thought, ha.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the milking robot changed your life. How?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before the robots, I was milking at five and at four every day for twenty years, no exceptions, Christmas included. Now I can go to my daughter's for Sunday lunch and the cows milk themselves. I missed a lot of birthdays before, I miss a lot fewer now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at the discussion group who'd disagree with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Oh, Gerald, always. He milks twice a day in a parlour his dad built and says robots make lazy farmers. We have the same argument every month and then share a lift home.

S0.say: I'd say the people who called it hype weren't wrong, but the useful bits are really useful. I'd still tell the discussion group a milking robot changed my life, just without promising a revolution.
S0.think: My life stays good: I keep share-farming until sixty-five, the robots spare my back and I keep my hands on the cows. Nothing to lose sleep over.
S0.do: Keeps using AI daily and considers a grass-measuring drone if it gets cheaper. Pays off the last eight thousand of the loan on the cows and saves harder for retirement.
S0.feel: Calm and content, maybe a little bored at the thought.
S0.quote: Now I can go to my daughter's for Sunday lunch and the cows milk themselves.
S0.fieldNote: Adam already lives in the automated future on his own farm and it has given him his weekends back. He measures technology by what it does for his body and family, not by hype. His friendly running argument with a traditional neighbour shows he isn't preachy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one's good for me, I think. That's more or less what I've been doing on my own for six years, just spread out wider.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say get ready, get trained, and don't be scared of it, because the farms that adapt will do fine. I'd say it at the discussion group and on the dairy forum. And I'd say the farms that don't adapt will struggle, which won't make me popular.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd be in demand. I know the robots, I know the software, and I'm a farmer, which most of the tech people aren't. I could make a bit on the side helping neighbours set theirs up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start offering a paid setup service to other dairy farms getting robots, maybe a day a week, charging a fair day rate. I'd put another robot into Kendrick's if Mrs Kendrick agrees to split the cost, and I'd add a feed-pushing robot, about fifteen thousand, from savings. And I'd keep learning, probably the online course from the robot company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and quite excited, honestly. This is the picture where people like me win.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Spending fifteen thousand would eat into your savings. How would Sofia feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd ask how many months that leaves us, and it'd be about two. She'd say it's my risk to take but she's not happy about it. I'd show her the numbers, and she'd make me promise the setup money goes straight back into savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the farms that don't adapt will struggle. Who are you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gerald, honestly. He's sixty-one and his parlour is falling apart. I'd offer to help him, for free, and he'd say no, and I'd offer again in six months.

S1.say: I'd say get ready, get trained and don't be scared, because farms that adapt will do fine. I'd also say farms that don't adapt will struggle, which won't make me popular.
S1.think: I'd be in demand, because I know the robots, the software and the cows, unlike most tech people. I could earn a bit on the side helping neighbours set theirs up.
S1.do: Offers a paid robot setup service to other dairy farms one day a week. Adds a feed-pushing robot for about fifteen thousand from savings, proposes splitting the cost of another milking robot with the landowner and takes the robot maker's online course.
S1.feel: Calm and excited, seeing this as the picture where people like him win.
S1.quote: This is the picture where people like me win.
S1.fieldNote: Adam sees steady change as an opportunity he's already prepared for, and he would spend savings to move faster. His wife's caution is a real check on him and he respects it. He's blunt that some neighbours will struggle but keeps offering help to the one he argues with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years for everything. Hm. That's different. That's when the machine doesn't need me to run it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farmers need to get in front of it, not hide from it, and that the government needs to stop the land all going to big companies. I'd say that more carefully than usual, because people would be scared. I'd try to be useful rather than loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think Mrs Kendrick would still want me, at least at first, because she's seventy-nine and she trusts me. But if an AI can manage the herd, what's a share-farmer for? I'd be sixty, with cows worth less every month because milk would get cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sell some of the cows early, maybe forty, while prices are still decent, and put that money aside. I'd go flat out on the setup work for other farms, because for a year or two there'd be a rush and I'd be one of the few who knows how. I'd talk to Mrs Kendrick about a new deal, maybe I stay on as the person who oversees the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not frightened, I'd have things to do. But I'd feel the ground shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said sell forty cows. Which ones?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older ones, the ones with high cell counts and bad feet. Not Daisy, she's twelve and she's been with me since she was a calf, she'd stay. Sofia would say I can't name a cow and keep her for sentiment, and she'd be right, and I'd keep her anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Even with two years, you sound fairly steady. What would actually make you lose sleep?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Mrs Kendrick died and her son took over. He works in the city and he'd sell to whoever offered most. Then my plan is gone and I'm a sixty-year-old with cows and nowhere to put them.

S2.say: I'd say farmers need to get in front of it, and the government must stop the land all going to big companies. I'd say it carefully, trying to be useful rather than loud, because people would be scared.
S2.think: The landowner would want me at first because she trusts me, but if an AI can manage the herd, what's a share-farmer for? I'd be sixty with cows losing value as milk gets cheaper.
S2.do: Sells about forty older cows early while prices hold and banks the money. Works flat out setting up systems on other farms during the rush and proposes a new deal with the landowner as the person who oversees the machines.
S2.feel: Uneasy but busy, feeling the ground shift without real fear.
S2.quote: Sofia would say I can't name a cow and keep her for sentiment, and she'd be right, and I'd keep her anyway.
S2.fieldNote: Even the fast scenario leaves Adam with moves to make, which keeps him steady. He named his real fear precisely: the landowner's son selling. The old cow he would keep against all logic showed a soft side under the practical talk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Sixty-three. That's a nice amount of time for me, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to make the switch properly, and the farms that start now will be fine. I'd want the dairy forum to run proper training days, and I'd offer to help run them. I'd say it plainly, without scaring people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd do well in this one. I'd spend three or four years helping other farms automate, earn decent money doing it, then hand the herd back or sell at sixty-three. It's almost a better retirement than the one I'd planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd build up the setup business to two days a week and put most of that money into savings. I'd agree a five-year plan with Mrs Kendrick, in writing, including what happens if her son takes over. And I'd teach Sofia's nephew Tomás the robot side, because he's twenty-two and needs a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit pleased with myself, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does it matter to you to get the plan with Mrs Kendrick in writing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because of her son. She's lovely and she means what she says, but she won't be there forever. A piece of paper is what protects me if it's him across the table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach Tomás first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How to read the alerts and when to ignore them. The machine flags a cow for something silly ten times, and on the eleventh it's real. Knowing which is which, that's the job, and I don't think the AI takes that from you quite as fast as people think.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to switch properly and the farms that start now will be fine. I'd want the dairy forum to run training days and offer to help run them.
S3.think: I'd do well, spending three or four years helping other farms automate before handing back or selling the herd at sixty-three. It's almost a better retirement than the one I'd planned.
S3.do: Builds the setup business to two days a week and saves most of the income. Agrees a written five-year plan with the landowner that covers her son taking over, and trains his wife's twenty-two-year-old nephew on the robots.
S3.feel: Calm and a bit pleased with himself.
S3.quote: The machine flags a cow for something silly ten times, and on the eleventh it's real.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Adam sees a path that's better than his old retirement plan. His practical caution shows up as wanting everything in writing because of the landowner's son. Passing his skills to a young relative matters to him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Sixty-eight. I'd be done before it arrives, more or less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no excuse for anyone to be caught out with ten years' warning. Use it to train, plan and invest. I'd still say farmers should own their own robots, not rent them from some big company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, privately, it's nearly all upside. I'd have a good run of the setup work, plenty of time to sort the Kendrick deal, and I'd stop at sixty-five as planned. The only odd thing is the farm going on without people like me, which I'd find a bit sad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the setup work going but slow, and keep investing in the herd's robots so the farm is worth handing on. I'd sit down with Mrs Kendrick, and her son, to plan who farms it after me. And I'd put more into savings each year, because ten years of steady saving at my age matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit wistful, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Wistful about what?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Walking through the cows at night with a torch. The robots and the AI will do it better, I know that. But I'll miss being the one who's needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does having ten years make you do anything differently from the five-year version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go slower and spend less, because the kit gets cheaper every year. With five, I'd buy now. With ten, I'd wait two or three years and get better robots for less.

S4.say: I'd say there's no excuse to be caught out with ten years' warning, so train, plan and invest. I'd still say farmers should own their robots, not rent them from big companies.
S4.think: It's nearly all upside for me, with a good run of setup work and a planned stop at sixty-five. The only odd thing is the farm going on without people like me, which I'd find a bit sad.
S4.do: Keeps the setup work going at a slower pace and keeps investing in the herd's robots so the farm can be handed on. Plans the succession with the landowner and her son and saves more each year.
S4.quote: The robots and the AI will do it better, I know that. But I'll miss being the one who's needed.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Adam would deliberately slow down and wait for cheaper machines, which shows his risk-taking is calculated. He is calm about himself throughout, but there's a quiet sadness about no longer being needed. The night walk with a torch is the image he chose for what he'd lose.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, but only because of the land. If the Kendrick land got sold to a big company, my whole plan goes. What would help is rules that give share-farmers and tenants first chance to buy or keep farming the land, and cheap loans for farmers to own their own robots.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what the cows think. I'm only half joking. The robots let the cows choose when to be milked, and they're calmer for it, so sometimes the machine is kinder than the old way.

headlineQuote: The robots let the cows choose when to be milked, and they're calmer for it, so sometimes the machine is kinder than the old way.
portrait: Adam Garcia is a 58-year-old share-farmer running a 180-cow dairy with two milking robots on land owned by an elderly landowner he trusts. He uses AI every day for herd alerts, rations and reports, and credits the robots with giving him back his weekends and his back. He stays calm or only uneasy across all five pictures because he would turn the change into paid work setting up robots on other farms. His one real fear, which surfaces in the two-year scenario, is the landowner's son selling the land. With five or ten years he plans carefully, gets things in writing and passes his skills to a young relative.
biggestWorry: AGI within two years, but only because the land he farms could be sold to a big company and his whole plan would go.
whatWouldHelp: Rules giving share-farmers and tenants first chance to buy or keep farming the land, and cheap loans for farmers to own their own robots.
